name: Ultherapy Prime

lead: Ultherapy Prime is the newer version of the Ultherapy skin-lifting device. Clinics use it for non-surgical lifting of the brow, lower face, under-chin and neck, and tightening of the decolletage.

Focused ultrasound, guided by live imaging, heats tiny points at chosen depths in the deep dermis and fascia. This is reported to stimulate new collagen and elastin and a tightening effect. Published data on the Prime model are so far early case series, a survey and a preprint; the wider MFU-V category is FDA-cleared for brow lifting, neck and submental tightening and decolletage wrinkles.

paras: A clinician performs it in a single office session, using the imaging screen to place energy at the right depths. Tightening develops gradually over the following months. People interested in jawline and neck definition often use it as a non-surgical option.
A 2025 survey compared patient-reported pain, redness and swelling between Prime and the older system. Treatment is performed by clinicians.

angle.text: Ultherapy Prime is used for non-surgical lifting of the lower face, jawline and neck. Focused ultrasound with live imaging heats deep tissue, prompting new collagen and tightening. Data on the Prime model are early; the original Ultherapy has a broader record.

lead: Ultherapy Prime is an updated version of the Ultherapy system, a noninvasive aesthetic device that uses microfocused ultrasound with real-time visualization (MFU-V) to tighten and lift skin. It is described in the literature as a second-generation system with an advanced processor and improved imaging compared with the original Ultherapy device.[1][2]

Microfocused ultrasound delivers energy to tiny points at different depths of the skin, producing thermal coagulation that is said to trigger a wound-repair response and the formation of new collagen and elastin.[3][4] A 2026 review states that MFU-V is cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration for brow lifting, neck and submental tightening and wrinkles of the decolletage, with additional clearance in 2025 for the abdomen and arms.[4]

In looksmaxxing culture the procedure is grouped with non-surgical hardmaxxing options for jawline and neck definition. Published evidence on the Prime model specifically is limited to early case series, a patient survey and company-linked comparison data, as listed below.

paras: Ultherapy Prime uses ultrasound imaging during treatment so the operator can see tissue layers before delivering energy. A preprint comparing the original system with Prime reported that the newer device has enhanced visualization and reduced visual noise.[2] A published pilot case series describes Prime as having an advanced processor and improved imaging.[1]
Treatment areas described in a survey of patients include the brow, the lax submental and neck areas, and lines on the decolletage.[3]

The Asia Pacific pilot case series notes that microfocused ultrasound with real-time visualization is established as a noninvasive lifting treatment, and states that Prime adds an advanced processor and improved imaging; the authors undertook the series because published Prime data in Asian patients were lacking.[1]

The preprint comparing the two generations states that its aim was to compare the visualization components and visual-noise reduction of the older and newer systems and to gather survey and case results from an early-experience program.[2]

Brow lifting, tightening of lax skin under the chin and along the neck, and improving lines on the decolletage are the uses named in the survey literature, and a 2026 Dermatologic Clinics review adds 2025 US clearance for the abdomen and arms.[3][4] For appearance purposes, treatment of the submental and neck region is the part people associate with a sharper jaw and neck angle, and brow treatment with a lifted brow line; both claim to change contour by tightening tissue rather than adding volume.[3][4]

Ultherapy Prime is positioned in the literature as an update to the original device, referred to in the preprint literature as MFU-V 1.0 versus MFU-V 2.0, with the later system described as offering enhanced visualization and processing capabilities, with potential gains in precision and patient comfort.[4][2]

Ultrasound energy is focused on small points at differing depths, creating thermal coagulation zones that are reported to induce neocollagenesis and elastin regeneration, producing a tightening and pulling effect in the deep dermis and fascia.[3][4]

A 2025 survey study compared patient-reported pain, erythema and edema after facial lifting with Ultherapy Prime and the older Ultherapy Legacy system.[3] A 2026 review of MFU-V discusses safety and technical considerations of the modality as a whole.[4]

The survey study asked patients to report pain, erythema and swelling after facial lifting with Prime or the older Legacy system, which are the effects usually discussed for the modality.[3] The 2026 review describes MFU-V as having a favorable safety profile across anatomic regions, while noting that the improved Prime processing may improve patient comfort.[4]

In looksmaxxing discussion the procedure is grouped with non-surgical options for jawline and neck definition and is compared with surgical lifts and with other energy devices; there are few forum threads specific to the Prime model, so most of the community framing is by category. Clinicians in the published material describe it as an in-clinic procedure performed by trained operators rather than a home device.[1][2]

A 2025 survey study compared patient-reported pain, erythema and edema between Ultherapy Prime and the Legacy system.[3] An Asia Pacific pilot case series described early experience with Prime, noting that published data in Asian patients had been lacking.[1] A 2025 preprint compared ultrasound visualization between the two systems and reported survey and case results from an early-experience program.[2]

Two trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov were recruiting at the time of writing: one examining long-term efficacy and duration of MFU-V at multiple depths (20 participants) and one examining visualization-guided treatment of the SMAS layer for facial laxity (50 participants).[5][6]

The pilot case series, survey and preprint are early-experience reports for the Prime model; the broader evidence base for microfocused ultrasound with visualization is summarised in the 2026 review of clinical applications, safety and technical considerations.[4][1][3][2]
